studies.label: Randomised crossover ideation experiment: public transport and university spaces

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 4, Sections 3.1 and 3.2.1; PDF p. 8, Table 4 note; PDF p. 9, Table 5 note
counts_source.quote: The study involved 51 third-year students from the bachelor’s degree in industrial design engineering and product development | Note. N= 102; Unaided n= 51. AI-assisted n= 51. | Note. N= 51; Group A n= 24. Group B n= 27.

arms.name: AI-assisted
arms.description: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) on university computers with internet access limited to ChatGPT. Group B receives AI first; Group A receives AI in the second task. Every participant completes one AI-assisted task.

arms.name: Unaided
arms.description: No computers, external resources, or electronic devices. Group A works unaided first; Group B works unaided after the AI-assisted task. Every participant completes one unaided task.

studies.task: Third-year industrial design engineering students generate eight innovative ideas in 30 minutes for public transport, then university spaces, documenting each idea with a handwritten description and drawing (PDF pp. 4-5, Sections 3.1 and 3.2.1).

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5)
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 5, Section 3.2.1; release year and model snapshot are not stated.

preregistration.where: No preregistration or registry is identified in the full article.

studies.shared_sample: Possible overlap with c201, DOI 10.1002/cae.22817, flagged by the reconciled screening form. The present paper cites that related study as prior work (PDF pp. 3, 13, 15) but does not establish whether participants overlap.

estimates.notes: Additional full-sample analysis of the same Existing Solutions outcome and participants as the paired Wilcoxon record. Mixed between-within ANOVA: ideation condition is the within-person factor and condition order the between-person factor (PDF p. 6, Section 3.3.1). This record preserves the AI-use main effect, Wilks lambda, and partial eta squared; it is not an independent sample. Arm means and SDs are the unadjusted values from Table 4. The reported partial eta squared is unsigned.

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Methods define average pairwise semantic divergence within each participant's own set of ideas; Results instead call it divergence from the centroid per participant. LaBSE embeddings of descriptions obtained using Gemini OCR with manual checking (PDF p. 7, Section 3.3.2; PDF pp. 10-11, Section 4.3 and Fig. 3).

sources.locator: PDF p. 10, Section 4.3, individual-level semantic divergence
sources.quote: At individual level, the average semantic divergence from the centroid per participant was M= 0.28 (SD = 0.03) for unaided ideas and M= 0.29 (SD = 0.03) for AI-assisted ideas.

estimates.notes: Printed means show greater divergence with AI, while the narrative describes lower divergence and greater homogenisation. Fig. 3 is consistent with the ordering of the printed means; no values were read from its plotted distributions. Signs of the printed test and effect size are preserved. The paper does not explicitly identify the confidence-interval target or the d standardizer, so ci_of and standardizer are null. Analysis-specific participant counts are not printed in this passage and are left null; degrees of freedom are not converted into participant counts. The stated paired analysis and participant-level definition conflict with the printed degrees of freedom. Participant-level SD coding follows the Results wording, but se_basis remains not_reported because the independent units cannot be confirmed. The disagreement between pairwise and centroid definitions also remains unresolved.

estimates.outcome: Group-level semantic divergence to the condition centroid
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Cosine distance of each idea description's LaBSE embedding from the mean embedding of its condition. Both tasks are pooled; text was extracted through Gemini OCR and manually verified (PDF p. 7, Section 3.3.2).

sources.locator: PDF p. 10, Section 4.3, group-level semantic divergence
sources.quote: At group level, the average semantic divergence to the centroid was M= 0.28 (SD = 0.06) for unaided ideas and M= 0.29 (SD = 0.07) for AI-assisted ideas.

sources.locator: PDF p. 5, Section 3.2.1, total submitted ideas

estimates.notes: Printed means show greater divergence with AI, while the narrative describes lower divergence and greater homogenisation. Fig. 3 is consistent with the ordering of the printed means; no values were read from its plotted distributions. Signs of the printed test and effect size are preserved. The paper does not explicitly identify the confidence-interval target or the d standardizer, so ci_of and standardizer are null. Analysis-specific participant counts are not printed in this passage and are left null; degrees of freedom are not converted into participant counts. The independent-samples test treats ideas as independent, although participants contribute several ideas and appear in both conditions; no participant adjustment is reported. The degrees of freedom also conflict with a conventional independent-samples test on the stated corpus. Within-person order was randomized, but this analysis is not a paired participant test, so within_person is null.

open_items: Semantic divergence: printed means and Fig. 3 show higher divergence with AI, but the abstract, Results, and Discussion describe lower divergence. Signs are preserved as printed; labels or interpretation require correction (PDF pp. 1, 10-11, 13).

Semantic analysis: the individual paired test prints t(364) despite the trial involving 51 people; the group test prints t(728) for the stated corpus of 728 ideas. Actual independent units and treatment of repeated observations are unresolved. Analysis-specific participant counts are left null for these two records (PDF pp. 4, 7, 10).

Individual semantic divergence is pairwise within each participant in Methods but described as distance from a centroid in Results and Fig. 3. The implemented metric and centroid need identification (PDF pp. 7, 10-11).

Neither semantic confidence interval is explicitly labelled as an interval for a raw difference or standardized effect, and the d standardizer is not stated. Printed intervals are retained with ci_of null (PDF p. 10).
No paired-difference SD, within-person correlation, or paired mean-difference SE is printed for the participant-level creativity outcomes. No paired precision has been derived (PDF pp. 8-9).

The diversity-index and category-richness comparisons have no printed SDs, SEs, intervals, or tests. Category-size and unique-contribution tests treat outputs as independent without a stated participant adjustment (PDF pp. 7, 9-10).
The category level used for the category-size comparison is not identified (PDF pp. 7, 10).
The text-elaboration word-counting method and image-elaboration scorer are not identified. Their measure codes remain null as in the reconciled screening form (PDF pp. 6-7, Table 2).
The ChatGPT/GPT-3.5 release year, model snapshot, and experiment date are not printed. ai_tool.year is null rather than inferred from external information (PDF p. 5 and full article).
Possible sample overlap with c201 / DOI 10.1002/cae.22817 is unresolved. The paper cites the related study but does not identify shared participants (PDF pp. 3, 13, 15).

The after-AI descriptives compare different tasks and periods, with no direct test of those two unaided cells. They do not identify a causal carryover effect; the limitation is established from the reported design (PDF pp. 5-6, 8-9).
notes: Extraction B, 2026-10-09. The full markdown conversion was read through the end of References. All tables and figures in the PDF were inspected before completing extraction; every cited numeric source was checked using pymupdf page text, with table recovery and page rendering for layout checks. No appendix, embedded supplement, or separate supplement on file was identified. Data availability says that data will be made available on request (PDF p. 15). Statistic inventory: participant creativity outcomes in Tables 4 and 5; the AI-usage main effect on Existing Solutions in Section 4.2; semantic divergence and category-size tests plus the separate chi-square tests in Section 4.3; exclusive categories and output event counts in Table 6; richness and four diversity indices in Table 7; and the printed total unique-contribution counts in Section 5.3. All descriptive unaided-cell comparisons mapped or noted by screening are retained separately as after-AI records. Counts are people unless specifically stored in n_units or raw output-count fields. The crossover has 51 distinct people: Group A has 24 and Group B has 27 (Table 5 note); Table 4 N = 102 counts repeated person-condition observations. Group A starts unaided and Group B starts with AI. The first task always concerns public transport and the second university spaces, so conditions were crossed but task order was fixed. Participant-level SD coding in Tables 4-5 follows the participant-based paired and group analyses; elaboration aggregation details are not separately specified. To preserve all printed quantities without converting counts into means, raw event totals use the additional stats keys treatment_count and control_count. Secondary printed Mann-Whitney z values and Wilks lambda use the additional test keys standardized_z and wilks_lambda. These extensions also have field-level source coverage. Set-level index and richness values occupy the usual arm-level fields, with unit set. No arm differences, rates, effect sizes, standard errors, or confidence limits were calculated. Source quotations retain the printed precision. The ANOVA main-effect record and Wilcoxon record concern the same outcome and participants and are alternative analyses, not independent estimates. Similarly, participant originality and output unique-contribution tests reuse the same coded ideas. Diversity outcomes aggregate both tasks; the same people contribute to both condition pools. Secondary-period and cross-period records retain their design limitations. No values were digitized from figures.
